meta.description: T.S. Eliot did write this line — in his 1931 preface to Harry Crosby's Transit of Venus. The popular version quietly drops one word: “just.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Eliot wrote this sentence — almost word for word — in his 1931 preface to Harry Crosby’s posthumous poetry collection Transit of Venus. The original reads “find out just how far one can go”; the popular internet version drops the word “just.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Preface to Transit of Venus: Poems, by Harry Crosby
Black Sun Press, Paris, November 1931 (limited edition of 500 copies)
“… can possibly find out just how far one can go.”

source.excerpt: Of course one can ‘go too far’ and except in directions in which we can go too far there is no interest in going at all; and only those who will risk going too far can possibly find out just how far one can go. Not to go far enough is to remain ‘in the vague’ as surely and less creditably than to exceed.
trail: Caresse Crosby commissioned the preface in 1930, after Harry Crosby’s death; Eliot sent the finished text to her in September 1931, and it was published by the Black Sun Press that November ↗.
The sentence is reprinted verbatim (with the word “just” intact) in the scholarly critical edition of Eliot’s prose, viewable as scanned pages 365–368 ↗.
Wikiquote’s T. S. Eliot page lists the line in its main quotes section, sourced to the Transit of Venus preface (1931) ↗, without flagging it as disputed.
A commenter on the WIST quotations database independently flagged the “just how far” discrepancy, noted on the site’s Eliot entry ↗.

author.name: T. S. Eliot
author.heading: About T. S. Eliot
author.bio: Thomas Stearns Eliot was a British-American poet, essayist, and playwright, and one of the most influential figures of literary modernism. He wrote The Waste Land (1922) and Four Quartets (1943), edited the literary journal The Criterion, worked for decades as an editor at Faber & Faber, and won the 1948 Nobel Prize in Literature.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Eliot is correct, but the wording circulating online is a slightly trimmed version of his actual sentence.

items.why: The popular quote reads “… can possibly find out how far one can go,” but Eliot’s original 1931 text reads “… can possibly find out just how far one can go” — the word “just” has been dropped, as documented on the WIST quotations database ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and nearly all the wording are genuinely Eliot’s, from his preface to Harry Crosby’s Transit of Venus (1931) — see the scanned original text ↗.

context.heading: A eulogy for a reckless poet
lead: Harry Crosby was an American poet, publisher (with his wife Caresse, of the Black Sun Press in Paris), and a fixture of the 1920s expatriate literary scene. He died in December 1929, in an apparent murder–suicide with his lover, at age 31. In 1930 Caresse Crosby asked T. S. Eliot — who had known the couple in Paris — to write a preface for a new edition of Harry’s collection Transit of Venus.

The preface is Eliot musing on poetic risk-taking: a poet who never over-reaches, he writes, “can go very far” only if willing to risk failure. The now-famous sentence appears near the end, as Eliot defends Crosby’s reach for a private symbolism: “Of course one can ‘go too far’ and except in directions in which we can go too far there is no interest in going at all; and only those who will risk going too far can possibly find out just how far one can go.”
detailsBody: Eliot himself was ambivalent about the piece: in a September 1931 letter to Caresse Crosby he called it dissatisfying, apologizing for its brevity and what he felt was its “poverty of ideas.” The book was published by the Black Sun Press in Paris in November 1931 in a limited edition.
